document_metadata.title: Never Split the Difference - Negotiating As If Your Life Depended On It
document_metadata.methodology: Chris Voss - Never Split the Difference

key_principles.name: Mirroring
key_principles.description: Mirroring is the practice of repeating the last 1-3 critical words someone just said to encourage them to elaborate further without feeling interrogated.
key_principles.when_to_use: When you want the prospect to continue talking and reveal more information, especially when they mention concerns, objections, or important details
key_principles.why_it_works: Creates a subconscious connection and makes the speaker feel heard, triggering them to naturally expand on their thoughts without defensive reactions
key_principles.sales_application: Use mirroring to get prospects to elaborate on pain points, budget constraints, decision criteria, or any concern they briefly mention

specific_examples.scenario: A SaaS prospect mentions they're concerned about implementation time
specific_examples.dialogue_example:
Prospect: 'We're worried the implementation will take too long and disrupt our team.'
Salesperson: 'Disrupt your team?'
Prospect: 'Yes, last time we implemented a new system, it took 3 months and our productivity dropped 40%.'

specific_examples.scenario: An insurance client discusses coverage concerns
specific_examples.dialogue_example:
Prospect: 'The deductible seems quite high for our situation.'
Salesperson: 'High for your situation?'
Prospect: 'Well, we have multiple properties and if we had claims on several, it would be expensive.'

specific_examples.scenario: A real estate buyer mentions location issues
specific_examples.dialogue_example:
Prospect: 'The location might not work for our employees.'
Salesperson: 'Not work for your employees?'
Prospect: 'Most of them live on the other side of town, adding 30 minutes to their commute.'

real_world_scenarios.scenario: During a demo when the prospect expresses concern about features or integration
When a buyer mentions issues with property price, location, or condition
When discussing coverage limits, deductibles, or premium costs

implementation_guide: Listen actively and identify the 1-3 most critical words in their statement
Repeat those words with an upward inflection, making it a question
Remain silent and maintain eye contact (or pause on phone), allowing them to elaborate
Take notes on the additional information they provide
Use the new information to ask deeper calibrated questions
common_mistakes_to_avoid: Mirroring too frequently - it becomes obvious and annoying
Repeating entire sentences instead of just key words
Using a mocking or sarcastic tone instead of genuine curiosity
Breaking the silence too quickly after mirroring

coaching_prompts.coach_prompt: 💡 Mirror their concern to get more details
coaching_prompts.salesperson_says: [Repeat their last 2-3 words as a question]

key_principles.name: Labeling
key_principles.description: Labeling is the practice of identifying and vocalizing someone's emotions to diffuse tension and build rapport through emotional acknowledgment.
key_principles.when_to_use: When emotions are evident but unspoken, when you need to defuse tension, or when you want to demonstrate empathy and understanding
key_principles.why_it_works: Acknowledging emotions validates the person's feelings, reduces their defensive stance, and creates psychological safety for open dialogue
key_principles.sales_application: Use labeling to address hidden concerns, defuse price objections, and navigate emotional resistance during negotiations

specific_examples.scenario: A prospect is confused about pricing structure
specific_examples.dialogue_example:
Prospect: 'This pricing doesn't make any sense to me.'
Salesperson: 'It seems like you're confused about how we structure our pricing.'
Prospect: 'Yes, I don't understand why there are so many tiers and add-ons.'

Prospect: 'I don't trust these ROI numbers you're showing.'
Salesperson: 'It sounds like you're skeptical about the projected returns.'
Prospect: 'Exactly, we've been burned by inflated promises before.'

Prospect: 'We can't afford this right now.'
Salesperson: 'It seems like budget is a real pressure point.'
Prospect: 'It is. We just had our funding cut by 20%.'

real_world_scenarios.scenario: When C-suite executives express skepticism about digital transformation
When administrators worry about disrupting patient care during implementation
When compliance officers express concerns about regulatory risks

implementation_guide: Observe verbal and non-verbal cues to identify the underlying emotion
Start with neutral third-party statements: 'It seems like...', 'It sounds like...', 'It looks like...'
Keep the label simple and focused on one emotion
Pause after labeling to allow them to confirm or correct
If wrong, gracefully accept correction: 'I misread that, help me understand...'
common_mistakes_to_avoid: Mislabeling emotions - always use tentative language
Being too direct or blunt with emotional observations
Labeling multiple emotions at once, creating confusion

coaching_prompts.salesperson_says: It seems like this is confusing
It seems like this is frustrating

key_principles.name: Tactical Empathy
key_principles.description: Tactical empathy is understanding and articulating the other person's emotions and perspective to influence outcomes while building genuine connection.
key_principles.when_to_use: When dealing with emotional resistance, building initial rapport, or when the prospect feels misunderstood or unheard
key_principles.why_it_works: Makes counterparts feel emotionally safe and understood, lowering their guard and creating openness to collaboration
key_principles.sales_application: Use tactical empathy to navigate emotional objections, build trust quickly, and transform adversarial dynamics into partnerships

specific_examples.dialogue_example:
Prospect: 'This whole vendor selection process is really frustrating.'
Salesperson: 'I hear your frustration. It sounds like you've been through this before without great results.'
Prospect: 'Exactly. We spent months last time and the solution didn't even work.'

Prospect: 'I'm worried about how the team will react to another change.'
Salesperson: 'Your concern about team morale is completely valid. Change fatigue is real.'
Prospect: 'Yes, we've had three system changes in two years.'

Prospect: 'We've been burned by vendors making big promises.'
Salesperson: 'I understand why past experiences would make you cautious about new vendors.'
Prospect: 'The last vendor promised the world and delivered nothing.'

real_world_scenarios.scenario: When IT teams resist another platform migration
When operations managers fear production disruption
When store managers worry about staff training requirements

implementation_guide: Listen for emotional undertones beyond the literal words
Acknowledge both the emotion and the reason behind it
Use phrases like 'I understand...', 'I hear...', 'That makes sense...'
Share similar experiences when appropriate to build connection
Avoid immediately jumping to solutions - sit with their emotion first
common_mistakes_to_avoid: Dismissing emotions to focus on logic
Moving too quickly from empathy to selling
Using fake or insincere empathy that feels manipulative

coaching_prompts.salesperson_says: I hear your frustration with this
I understand why you'd be cautious

key_principles.name: Calibrated Questions
key_principles.description: Calibrated questions are open-ended 'How' and 'What' questions that give the illusion of control while guiding counterparts to your desired outcome.
key_principles.when_to_use: When facing objections, ensuring implementation, or when you need the prospect to think through solutions themselves
key_principles.why_it_works: Shifts mental focus from confrontation to collaboration, making counterparts feel autonomous while working toward your goals
key_principles.sales_application: Use calibrated questions to handle price objections, uncover hidden obstacles, and ensure commitment to implementation

specific_examples.dialogue_example:
Prospect: 'That solution won't work for our team.'
Salesperson: 'What would work better for your situation?'
Prospect: 'We'd need something that integrates with our existing CRM and doesn't require coding.'

Prospect: 'The price is way too high for us.'
Salesperson: 'How can we make this work within your budget?'
Prospect: 'Maybe if we could phase the implementation or adjust the payment terms...'

specific_examples.scenario: Prospect needs to think about it
specific_examples.dialogue_example:
Prospect: 'I need to think about this.'
Salesperson: 'What specifically concerns you most?'
Prospect: 'I'm not sure my team has the bandwidth to implement this quarter.'

real_world_scenarios.scenario: When clients resist recommendations that require organizational change
When hospitals cite budget constraints for new equipment
When schools worry about teacher adoption of new platforms

implementation_guide: Start questions with 'How' or 'What' - avoid 'Why' which sounds accusatory
Frame questions to make them problem-solve for mutual benefit
Use questions like: 'How can we resolve this?', 'What would need to change?'
Let them talk through their answer without interrupting
Build on their answers with follow-up calibrated questions
common_mistakes_to_avoid: Using 'Why' questions which trigger defensiveness
Asking closed-ended questions that get yes/no answers
Asking multiple questions at once, creating confusion

coaching_prompts.coach_prompt: 💡 Ask how to make it work
coaching_prompts.salesperson_says: How can we make this work?

key_principles.name: Accusation Audit
key_principles.description: An accusation audit involves listing every negative thing your counterpart could think about you upfront to trigger their empathy and disarm objections.
key_principles.when_to_use: At the beginning of difficult conversations, before delivering bad news, or when you expect strong resistance
key_principles.why_it_works: Triggers psychological reactance where people want to disagree with negative assessments, making them defend you instead of attack
key_principles.sales_application: Use accusation audits before price discussions, when entering competitive situations, or addressing service failures

specific_examples.dialogue_example:
Salesperson: 'You probably think we're the most expensive option, that we're overpriced, and that we don't understand your budget constraints.'
Prospect: 'Well, I wouldn't say that. I know quality comes at a price.'

Salesperson: 'You might think we're too small, too new, and that switching from your current vendor would be too risky.'
Prospect: 'Not necessarily. We're open to better solutions regardless of company size.'

Salesperson: 'You probably think we're unreliable, that we don't value your time, and that this delay shows we can't deliver.'
Prospect: 'Look, delays happen. What matters is how you handle them.'

real_world_scenarios.scenario: When pitching against Fortune 500 competitors
When your rates are higher than competitors
When you lack certain features competitors have

implementation_guide: List 3-5 worst things they could think about you or your offer
Deliver calmly without defensiveness or self-pity
Use phrases like 'You probably think...', 'You might believe...'
Pause after the audit to let them respond
Don't argue if they agree with some points - acknowledge and move forward
common_mistakes_to_avoid: Being too negative and talking yourself out of the deal
Overdoing the audit and seeming manipulative
Defending yourself immediately after the audit

coaching_prompts.salesperson_says: You might think others are better
You probably think we dropped the ball

key_principles.name: Dynamic Silence
key_principles.description: Dynamic silence is the strategic use of pauses to create space for the other person to fill with valuable information and concessions.
key_principles.when_to_use: After making an offer, asking a question, or when the prospect pauses mid-thought
key_principles.why_it_works: Creates productive discomfort that compels people to fill the void, often revealing hidden information or making concessions
key_principles.sales_application: Use silence after price quotes, following questions, and when prospects are processing information

specific_examples.dialogue_example:
Salesperson: 'The investment for this solution is $50,000.' [Remains silent for 5 seconds]
Prospect: 'That's... actually less than I expected. We budgeted $60,000.'

Prospect: 'Well, the thing is...' [trails off]
Salesperson: [Remains silent, maintaining eye contact]
Prospect: '...we're actually looking to replace our current vendor by Q2.'

Salesperson: 'Are you ready to move forward?' [Silence]
Prospect: [After 4 seconds] 'Yes, but we need to start with a smaller pilot first.'

real_world_scenarios.scenario: After presenting an offer on a property
After stating the final price on a vehicle
After asking for a multi-year commitment

implementation_guide: Count to 5 slowly in your head before speaking
Maintain calm, neutral body language during silence
On phone calls, resist the urge to fill dead air
If they ask 'Are you still there?' simply say 'Yes, I'm listening'
Use silence after every important question or statement
common_mistakes_to_avoid: Breaking silence too quickly due to discomfort
Appearing uncomfortable or fidgeting during silence
Using silence punitively or manipulatively

key_principles.name: Black Swan Discovery
key_principles.description: Black Swan discovery is the practice of uncovering hidden, game-changing information that completely shifts the negotiation dynamics in your favor.
key_principles.when_to_use: When something doesn't add up, when facing unexpected resistance, or when you sense hidden factors affecting the decision
key_principles.why_it_works: Reveals unknown unknowns - information you didn't know you didn't know - that can completely transform the negotiation
key_principles.sales_application: Use black swan discovery to uncover hidden budgets, undisclosed deadlines, political dynamics, or competitive situations

specific_examples.dialogue_example:
Prospect: 'We need to wait until next quarter.'
Salesperson: 'What specifically happens next quarter?'
Prospect: 'That's when our merger completes and we'll have the combined budget.'

Prospect: 'We need this implemented by March 15th.'
Salesperson: 'What makes March 15th so critical?'
Prospect: 'That's when our biggest client audits our systems.'

Prospect: 'I just can't move forward right now.'
Salesperson: 'What aren't you telling me?'
Prospect: 'Honestly? The CEO's son is pushing a different solution.'

real_world_scenarios.scenario: When decision-making stalls despite stakeholder agreement
When procurement processes have hidden requirements
When portfolio companies have undisclosed exit timelines

implementation_guide: Look for inconsistencies between words and actions
Ask 'What else?' repeatedly to dig deeper
Use phrases like 'What aren't you telling me?' when appropriate
Pay attention to what they're NOT saying
Create psychological safety for them to reveal sensitive information
common_mistakes_to_avoid: Being too aggressive in probing for information
Missing subtle cues that indicate hidden factors
Asking about black swans too early before building trust

key_principles.name: Anchoring with Precision
key_principles.description: Anchoring uses precise, odd numbers and specific terms to establish psychological reference points that influence the entire negotiation.
key_principles.when_to_use: When discussing price, terms, timelines, or any quantifiable aspect of the deal
key_principles.why_it_works: Precise numbers appear calculated and researched, making them seem less negotiable and more credible than round numbers
key_principles.sales_application: Use precise anchoring for pricing, payment terms, implementation timelines, and service levels

specific_examples.dialogue_example:
Prospect: 'What's your best price for this?'
Salesperson: 'We can do this for $47,850.'
Prospect: 'That's very specific. How did you arrive at that number?'

Prospect: 'How long will implementation take?'
Salesperson: 'We'll have you fully operational in 73 days.'
Prospect: 'That's precise. You must have done this before.'

Prospect: 'Can you do any better on price?'
Salesperson: 'I can offer a 13.7% discount if you sign this week.'
Prospect: 'That's an odd percentage. Is that your limit?'

real_world_scenarios.scenario: When proposing project fees and timelines
When offering annual contract discounts
When negotiating bulk order pricing

implementation_guide: Use odd, precise numbers like $4,827 instead of $5,000
Decrease increments when making concessions (20%, then 10%, then 5%)
Provide ranges with precise anchors: '$4,827 to $5,243'
Support precise numbers with brief logic when asked
Never use round numbers for final offers
common_mistakes_to_avoid: Using round numbers that invite further negotiation
Making large price movements that seem arbitrary
Being unable to explain your precise numbers if asked

conversation_starters.opener: Hi [Name], I know you weren't expecting my call. Do you have 27 seconds for me to tell you why I'm calling?
conversation_starters.purpose: Gets permission and sets time expectation
conversation_starters.follow_up: If yes: brief value prop. If no: 'When would be a better time?'

conversation_starters.opener: Thanks for taking the time. Before we dive in, what's your biggest challenge with [relevant area] right now?
conversation_starters.purpose: Immediately focuses on their pain points
conversation_starters.follow_up: Mirror or label their response to go deeper

conversation_starters.opener: I've prepared some specific examples based on our last conversation. But first, what's changed since we last spoke?
conversation_starters.purpose: Checks for new information before presenting
conversation_starters.follow_up: Adjust demo based on their update

conversation_starters.opener: Before we discuss investment levels, help me understand: what would make this a no-brainer decision for you?
conversation_starters.purpose: Uncovers their value drivers before price anchor
conversation_starters.follow_up: Frame pricing in context of their stated value

objection_handlers.response: It seems like budget is a real concern for you. Help me understand - too expensive compared to what?
objection_handlers.example_dialogue:
Prospect: 'Your solution is too expensive.'
Salesperson: 'Too expensive? (pause) It seems like budget is tight right now. What would need to change for this to make sense financially?'
Prospect: 'Well, if we could see ROI within 6 months...'

objection_handlers.objection: We need to think about it
objection_handlers.response: I understand you need time to process. What specifically do you need to think through?
objection_handlers.example_dialogue:
Prospect: 'We need to think about this.'
Salesperson: 'Of course. What specific concerns do you need to address internally?'
Prospect: 'Mainly whether our team has bandwidth for the implementation.'

objection_handlers.objection: We're happy with our current vendor
objection_handlers.response: Sounds like they're taking good care of you. What would have to change for you to consider alternatives?
objection_handlers.example_dialogue:
Prospect: 'We're satisfied with our current solution.'
Salesperson: 'Satisfied with current? (pause) What would make you open to exploring alternatives?'
Prospect: 'Only if they couldn't scale with our growth plans.'

objection_handlers.objection: I don't have authority to decide
objection_handlers.response: I appreciate your honesty. Who else needs to weigh in, and what would they want to know?
objection_handlers.example_dialogue:
Prospect: 'I can't make this decision alone.'
Salesperson: 'I understand. How does the decision process work here? What would your CEO need to see?'
Prospect: 'She'd want to see the ROI calculation and integration plan.'

closing_techniques.name: The Calibrated Close
closing_techniques.when_to_use: When they've expressed interest but haven't committed
closing_techniques.exact_words: How do we move forward together on this?
closing_techniques.fallback: What would need to happen for you to feel comfortable moving forward?

closing_techniques.name: The Implementation Close
closing_techniques.exact_words: What's our first step after you sign?
closing_techniques.fallback: How do you see the rollout happening on your end?

closing_techniques.name: The Assumption Close
closing_techniques.exact_words: When should we schedule the kickoff call?

discovery.focus: Uncover pain points and build rapport
quick_prompts: Ask: 'How are you handling this now?'
Say: 'It seems like price is a concern'
Audit: 'You probably think this is risky'
Ask: 'How can we solve this together?'
Ask: 'How can we make this work?'
Ask: 'What stops us from moving forward?'

responses: Say: 'What would they want to know?'
